Part 1

Why layers, and when does a layer count?

Part 1 · the plan

Seven layers, their limits, and independence

  1. Inherent safety firstwhat the process itself contributes
  2. The onionseven layers and what each needs to work
  3. Operating windowstarget, alarm, trip and critical limit
  4. Independencea shared transmitter fails two layers at once

Step 1 · layer 0

The process is the first layer

What CR-201 gets for free

  • Ammonium sulphate: no fire, no toxic cloud.
  • Boiling at 60 °C under 13.5 kPa a vacuum.
  • Supersaturation made by flashing, not on hot tubes.

What it still holds

    Inherent features remove whole hazards; every outer layer only manages what is left.

    Step 2 · interactive · pick a layer

    Each layer needs different things to work

    Layers 1–3 need power and a computer; layers 4–5 need neither.

    Step 3 · interactive · move the value

    Alarm before trip, trip before harm

    Level and heater have a trip; CR-201 pressure has only an alarm before its design limit.

    Step 4 · interactive · pick a hazard

    Does the trip share a sensor with the loop?

    Overfill has its own switch; the heater trips read the control transmitters.

    Part 1 · summary

    What Part 1 settled

    • Inherent safety removes hazards; layers manage the rest.
    • Seven layers, each with its own needs and weak points.
    • A window orders target, alarm, trip and critical limit.
    • A layer counts only if independent of the cause.

    Next: the three instrumented layers at work.

    2

    Part 2

    How do control, alarms and the SIS share the work?

    Part 2 · the plan

    Timing, fail positions, logic and voting

    1. Layers in actionfour deviations run on the model
    2. Fail positionswhere each valve goes without air
    3. Cause and effectwhat each trip closes
    4. Voting1oo1, 1oo2, 2oo2, 2oo3

    Step 1 · interactive · pick a deviation

    How much time does each layer get?

    Overfill leaves the operator 35 min before LSHH-201; the heater leaves 14 s, too short for alarm credit.

    Step 2 · interactive · cut the instrument air

    Every valve goes to a chosen position

    PV-202 fails open on purpose: losing vacuum stops the boiling, which is the safe state.

    Step 3 · interactive · pick a cause

    I-1 shuts the unit, I-2 only the heat

    I-1 latches and needs a manual reset; I-2 closes XV-301 and leaves the feed on.

    Step 4 · simplified IEC 61508

    More sensors: fewer missed demands, or fewer false trips

    $$\text{1oo1: } \tfrac{\lambda T}{2}\qquad \text{1oo2: } \tfrac{(\lambda T)^2}{3}+\beta\tfrac{\lambda T}{2}\qquad \text{2oo2: } \lambda T\qquad \text{2oo3: } (\lambda T)^2+\beta\tfrac{\lambda T}{2}$$

    $\lambda$ dangerous undetected failure rate, $T$ proof-test interval, $\beta$ common-cause share.

    1oo2: either sensor trips; a single failure cannot block the tripsafer, more spurious
    2oo2: both must agree; one failed sensor blocks itfewer spurious, less safe

    Step 4 · interactive · sensor voting

    Common cause caps what redundancy buys

    At $\beta$ = 10 % a second sensor gains about one decade: common cause, not the sensor count, sets the floor.

    Part 2 · summary

    What Part 2 settled

    • Alarm credit needs time: 35 min on overfill, seconds on the heater.
    • Fail positions are a design choice, valve by valve.
    • I-1 shuts feed and steam; I-2 only the steam.
    • Voting trades safety against spurious trips; common cause limits both.

    Next: the layers that need no power and no logic.

    3

    Part 3

    What acts when the instruments have failed?

    Part 3 · the plan

    Relief, containment, emergency response, audit

    1. The layered P&IDrelief, containment and response items
    2. The relief gapwhy CR-201 needs a device
    3. A good-practice auditOK, check or gap

    Step 1 · interactive · pick an outer layer

    Most outer-layer items are still recommendations

    14 of 17 outer-layer items are recommendations: the P&ID shows almost none of them.

    Step 2 · layer 4

    Full-vacuum design covers one side only

    CaseWhat protects CR-201 nowRecommended
    Vacuum (ejector, cooling)Rated for full vacuum: no device neededConfirm every part (R02)
    Steam tube rupture in E-301Operator on PIC-202 HI onlyRelief device (R01), PSHH (LR1)
    Blocked outlet, steam-outNothing passiveRestriction orifice (LR2)
    Slurry at the relief inlet—Rupture disc or flushed nozzle

    Design pressure is 1 bar g: a steam leak into a sealed vessel can exceed it.

    Step 3 · interactive · filter by status

    Eleven checks against good practice

    The gaps sit in timing, relief and emergency response: the LOPA and SRS decks size the fixes.

    Part 3 · summary

    What Part 3 settled

    • Relief and containment act on physics alone.
    • CR-201 has no relief device for overpressure yet.
    • Emergency response protects people, not the plant.
    • The audit names the gaps the next studies size.

    Layers are listed; next, LOPA asks whether they are enough.

    This deck

    Key Takeaways

    1

    Design out the hazard first; layers manage what remains.

    2

    A layer counts only if independent, effective and in time.

    3

    Shared transmitters and short process safety times are the weak points.

    4

    Passive relief is missing on CR-201 overpressure: close R01.
